interactions.summary: Jiang rejects passive waiting and invites another contribution while the class searches for an answer inside the present world.
A student proposes that Dante's destiny simplifies his worldview, making simplicity itself feel closer to God and love.
Jiang endorses that reading and says prophecy gives Dante focus: doubt, ego, and fear fall away once his contingent will aligns with absolute will around finishing the Divine Comedy.
A student asks whether Dante's suffering is still part of a plan if free human persecution was the very thing that made his journey and poem possible.
Jiang replies that Dante can forgive because he recognizes that everything has a purpose once he achieves his own.
The student then asks whether Dante could still have achieved his purpose without persecution.
Jiang answers no: exile and isolation were necessary conditions for writing the Divine Comedy, which leads the student to restate that Dante needed persecution in order to become the poet.

claims.claim: A student suggests that embracing destiny simplifies Dante's whole worldview, and that this simplicity feels close to both God and love.
Jiang says prophecy gives Dante total focus by stripping away doubt, ego, and fear, so that his contingent will comes into alignment with absolute will.
Jiang says prophecy matters because it gives Dante the future and lets him know his place in the universe.
Jiang says Dante can forgive others by recognizing that everything has a purpose as long as he fulfills his own purpose.
Jiang says Dante would not have achieved his purpose without exile, because the Divine Comedy required isolation and persecution created that condition.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang presents prophecy as an engine of concentration: once Dante knows his task, doubt, ego, and fear collapse into focus.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It converts providence from abstract foreknowledge into a practical transformation of will.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang uses a strong metaphysical formula to describe Dante's conversion of purpose: the absolute will and the contingent will become the same thing.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the absolute will is now the contingent will as well
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is one of the lecture's densest formulations of alignment between divine order and personal vocation.

signature_moments.moment: The class lands on a stark necessity claim: without exile and isolation, there is no Divine Comedy.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sharply ties persecution, poetic vocation, and providence together instead of treating exile as accidental background suffering.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The student uses simplicity to name the clarified, God-adjacent orientation that appears once Dante embraces destiny.
Jiang's phrase for the higher or divine will that prophecy brings into alignment with Dante's contingent personal will.
Purpose here names the vocation whose fulfillment retroactively gives meaning to suffering and makes forgiveness possible.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-06-17 Jiang pushes the providence argument into a stronger teleological form: prophecy simplifies Dante, aligns his will with a higher will, and makes exile a necessary condition for the poem rather than a merely regrettable detour.

uncertainty_notes.note: The student's long question is syntactically broken, but the stable pressure is clear: persecution appears both freely chosen and somehow necessary for Dante's vocation.
